title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
This report presents results from Phase 2 of the NCC access inequalities analysis: survival modelling of the time from birth to NCC admission. Where the Phase 1 logistic models asked whether a baby is admitted to NCC, this analysis asks how quickly — and specifically, whether some groups experience delayed access.
The key innovation is restricting the analysis to babies who were admitted to NCC (i.e., babies we know needed critical care). This isolates the pure timing/delay question from the access question already answered by Phase 1.
Key findings:

No systematic ethnic delay: Among babies admitted to NCC, all ethnic groups are admitted at similar speed after clinical adjustment. No group shows a statistically significant delay relative to White British babies.
No deprivation gradient: Deprivation has no effect on admission timing — all IMD quintiles show HR ≈ 1.0.
Unit type matters: Babies born at LNU sites are admitted ~3% faster than those at NICUs (HR 1.03, p=0.008), likely reflecting the simpler local admission pathway.
Hospital variation is negligible: The frailty variance dropped to near-zero (0.00003), compared with an ICC of ~32% in the logistic model. Hospitals differ in who they admit, not how fast.







ImportantKey Messages




Once the decision to admit is made, NCC access is equitable. Ethnicity and deprivation do not delay admission. Clinicians’ assertion that care is guided by signs and symptoms — not demographics — is supported by the data.
The inequality sits upstream. Phase 1 showed that hospital variation and modest ethnicity effects influence whether a baby enters NCC. Phase 2 shows that once admitted, the process is fair. The intervention point is the admission threshold, not the admission process.
Unit designation shapes the pathway. LNU sites admit slightly faster than NICUs — consistent with local, same-hospital admissions versus the more complex transfers and stabilisation involved at tertiary centres.

title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
2.1 Study Population
The analysis includes babies born in England during FY 2023/24 who were admitted to NCC at a hospital within a recognised NNAP neonatal unit. The NNAP filter restricts to 134 delivery sites across 105 NHS trusts with designated neonatal units (NICU, LNU, or SCBU), as identified from the NNAP 2024 unit data.

Primary analysis (Model 6): 42,425 NCC admissions with complete data on gestation, ethnicity, IMD, and delivery unit type
Sensitivity analysis (Model 7): 23,622 admissions with additional birth weight and Apgar data

title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
2.2 Outcome
Time from birth to NCC admission (hours). All babies in this analysis have the event — the outcome is when, not whether. Times are capped at 28 days (672 hours); admissions beyond this are treated as data linkage artefacts. Times ≤0 hours are set to 0.1 (6 minutes) to represent same-hour admission.

title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
2.3 Statistical Approach
We fitted Cox proportional hazards models with a shared frailty term (random intercept) for delivery site — the survival analysis analogue of the mixed-effects logistic model from Phase 1.
Model 6 (Primary): \[h(t) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp(\beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_3 \text{IMD} + \beta_4 \text{UnitType} + w_j)\]
Model 7 (Sensitivity): \[h(t) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp(\beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{BirthWeight} + \beta_3 \text{Apgar} + \beta_4 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_5 \text{IMD} + \beta_6 \text{UnitType} + w_j)\]
where \(w_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_w)\) is the shared frailty for delivery site \(j\), and \(h_0(t)\) is the baseline hazard.






NoteInterpreting Hazard Ratios



HR > 1 means faster admission (event occurs sooner). HR < 1 means slower admission (potential delay). This is the opposite intuition to odds ratios — a higher hazard ratio is the “better” outcome here.

title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
2.4 Unit Type Classification
Each delivery site is classified by its highest neonatal unit designation:

NICU (Level 3): Neonatal Intensive Care Unit — provides the full range of medical and surgical neonatal care
LNU (Level 2): Local Neonatal Unit — provides high dependency and some short-term intensive care
SCBU (Level 1): Special Care Baby Unit — provides special care for the least unwell babies

Unit type is included as a fixed effect (reference: NICU). The hospital-level frailty captures residual variation after accounting for unit type.

title: Inequalities in NCC Access: Survival Analysis Results
text:
8.1 Implications
The inequality in NCC access sits at the admission threshold, not the admission process. The intervention point is:

Standardising admission criteria across hospitals — the ICC of ~32% in Phase 1 suggests that clinical decision-making about NCC admission varies substantially by hospital. This is where most inequality enters the system.
Investigating specific ethnic effects at the hospital level — the modest national-level effects for Pakistani and Chinese babies in Phase 1 may concentrate in specific hospitals or networks.
Recognising equitable care delivery — once the admission decision is made, the NHS neonatal system delivers equitable speed-of-access regardless of ethnicity, deprivation, or hospital. This is a positive finding that validates current clinical practice.







TipCaveat on Timing Resolution



The majority of NCC admissions occur within the first hour of birth. With such a compressed time distribution, the power to detect small ethnic differences in timing is limited. The absence of a statistically significant delay is reassuring but does not rule out very small differences (e.g., minutes) that this analysis cannot resolve.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care
text:
3.1 Phase 1: Hierarchical Logistic Regression
We fitted mixed-effects logistic regression models with random intercepts for delivery trust, asking whether the probability of NCC admission varies by ethnicity and deprivation after adjusting for clinical need. (See the Phase 1 Methods section for why we cluster at trust rather than site level.)

Primary model: Adjusts for gestation, ethnicity (9 disaggregated groups), and IMD quintile, with trust random intercepts (~476,000 births — the full cohort of 506,656 less records missing gestation, ethnicity or IMD)
Sensitivity model: Additionally adjusts for birth weight and Apgar 5-minute score (~219,000 births with complete clinical data)

This two-model design lets the primary model run on nearly the whole cohort, while the sensitivity model checks the findings hold with fuller clinical adjustment. Ethnicity is coded using disaggregated NHS categories (Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi separately, rather than a single “Asian” group); the results bear this choice out, since these groups differ materially.
Both are mixed-effects (multilevel) models: each trust gets its own baseline admission rate, and the ethnicity and deprivation effects are estimated within trusts. This matters because baseline NCC admission rates vary widely between hospitals — through clinical thresholds, capacity and reporting practice. Without the hospital baseline in the model, a group of babies concentrated in high-admitting hospitals would look over-admitted when the effect is really the hospital’s, not the group’s. The estimates therefore answer a like-for-like question: for two clinically similar babies born in the same trust, does the chance of admission differ by ethnicity or deprivation?

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.1 Study Population
Primary analysis: 476,475 hospital births in England during financial year 2023/24 with complete data on NCC admission, gestation, ethnicity, IMD quintile, and delivery trust.
Sensitivity analysis: 218,886 births (45.9% of primary sample) with additional complete data on birth weight and Apgar 5-minute score.
The cohort is defined by birth in 2023/24, not by NCC activity in 2023/24. Babies enter on the basis of their MSDS birth record (the financial year is derived from year and month of birth); a baby born before April 2023 who continued a neonatal stay into the study year is not included. Critical-care linkage then looks outward from each birth — and is permitted to reach about 30 days into 2024/25 — so that NCC admissions for babies born late in March 2024 are not under-counted; but the linkage never pulls earlier-born babies into the cohort.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.5 Statistical Approach
We fitted three models:

Model 1 (Fixed effects only): Standard logistic regression adjusting for gestation, ethnicity, and deprivation. Retained as a reference point; estimates are in the technical appendix.
Model 2 (Mixed effects, gestation only): Hierarchical logistic regression with random intercepts for delivery trust, adjusting only for gestation among clinical covariates \[\text{logit}(P[\text{NCC}]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_3 \text{IMD} + u_j\] where \(u_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\) represents the random effect for delivery trust \(j\). Reported because it uses the maximum sample size (gestation is near-completely observed).
Model 3 (Mixed effects, full clinical adjustment): Adds birth weight and Apgar 5-minute score to Model 2’s specification \[\text{logit}(P[\text{NCC}]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{BirthWeight} + \beta_3 \text{Apgar} + \beta_4 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_5 \text{IMD} + u_j\]

Conceptually Model 3 is the preferred specification — it adjusts for the clinical case-mix that drives NCC need rather than relying on gestation alone — and we lead the interpretation with its results. Model 2 is reported in parallel because of its larger sample (gestation is observed for nearly all births, whereas birth weight and Apgar are observed for 45.9% of the primary sample). Where the two models disagree (notably for Pakistani and Indian ethnic groups), the disagreement itself is informative and is discussed below.

The table rules out the first two mechanisms for all four outliers:

Their field completeness is unremarkable: 93–99% of their births carry all three model fields (nationally 94%), and each trust’s crude NCC rate is essentially unchanged when restricted to the model-usable subset. Complete-case selection is not what lifts them out of the funnel.
A third explanation also fails on arithmetic: referral activity cannot raise a trust’s position in a delivery-cohort funnel. The funnel counts babies born at each trust, and over 99% of the NCC recorded for those babies was provided by the delivery trust itself. Transfers into a tertiary unit never enter its numerator here.

What remains — and what the right-hand columns show — is the third data mechanism. At the outlier trusts, 21–40% of term (≥37-week) babies carry an NCC record, against ~7% everywhere else, while their preterm birth shares are unremarkable (7.7–8.7%, national 7.9%). Expected admissions are the population-average (case-mix only) predictions from the primary model with the trust random effect removed (predict(..., re.form = NA)), aggregated per trust and indirectly standardised so the national observed/expected ratio is 1. Control limits use the standard funnel formulation (Spiegelhalter, Statistics in Medicine, 2005): on the standardised-ratio scale the limits are \(1 \pm z\sqrt{\phi}/\sqrt{E}\), shown here multiplied by the national crude rate.
Because between-trust variation here is far larger than binomial sampling noise (the same signal as the ICC), the limits include a multiplicative overdispersion factor \(\phi\), estimated from the winsorised standardised residuals so that a handful of extreme trusts do not themselves inflate it. Without this adjustment almost every trust would fall outside the limits — a true reflection of the large ICC, but useless for isolating individual outliers. Even so, the same data-quality caveats apply as to the ICC: MSDS / PbR-CC submission completeness varies between providers, so outliers should be read as flags for follow-up, not as confirmed differences in admission practice. The completeness diagnostic above shows how to separate these readings — for the current outliers the evidence points to numerator breadth in the PbR-CC return rather than either missing records or missing fields.

After adjusting for gestation and comparing within trusts, most ethnic groups sit within a few percent of parity with White British babies (full estimates in the Model 2 table and Figure 1). The Black group sits at near-exact parity; Pakistani and Chinese babies sit below parity in this model; Indian and Bangladeshi babies sit slightly above. The Pakistani estimate is largely a case-mix finding: the lower odds in the primary model move to near-parity once birth weight and Apgar are adjusted for. The Indian and Bangladeshi estimates move further above parity, suggesting NCC use at least proportionate to clinical need. The differences among Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi babies after adjustment are the clearest demonstration of why this report uses disaggregated ethnicity coding.
The Chinese group is the largest unexplained deviation: around 24% lower odds remain after clinical adjustment (the BH-adjusted p-value in the Model 2 table is the appropriate test of evidence). At least five explanations are consistent with this, and the data cannot separate them:

Residual case-mix confounding — Chinese babies have lower mean birth weight at term in UK data, and a single linear birth-weight term may not fully capture this.
Lower upstream clinical risk — different maternal age structure, parity distribution, or rates of high-risk pregnancy.
Sample size — Chinese is one of the smaller ethnic groups in the cohort, so the estimate is less stable than the odds ratio alone suggests.
Care-seeking and access differences — different patterns of antenatal engagement, including selective use of private antenatal care.
Ascertainment — possible under-recording of NCC episodes in this group, though there is no direct evidence for this.

Distinguishing these would need richer clinical covariates or direct engagement with providers (see Recommendations). The estimate should be treated as a question rather than a conclusion.

4.2.1 A broad, MBRRACE-comparable grouping
MBRRACE-UK reports present their headline ethnicity findings using broad groups (White, Mixed, Asian, Black, Other), and it is a fair question whether the ten-category grouping used here is more detailed than the data can support. To allow direct comparison, the primary model was refitted on the same 476,475 births with ethnicity collapsed to the five broad ONS groups; every other part of the model specification is unchanged. The multiple-testing cost of the extra detail is handled explicitly (Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment within the ethnicity family), and MBRRACE itself disaggregates beyond the broad groups in its extended tables where numbers allow. 4.4 Deprivation
The deprivation gradient suggests babies from more deprived areas have higher odds of NCC admission:
Babies from the most deprived quintile have 2% higher odds of NCC admission than the least deprived, and the gradient steps up consistently across quintiles. Two interpretations are worth separating explicitly, because they carry different implications:

Deprivation as a proxy for unmeasured need (the most likely reading). Our clinical adjustment — gestation, and in the sensitivity model birth weight and Apgar — almost certainly does not capture the full excess morbidity carried by babies from the most deprived areas. On this reading the gradient is the model responding correctly to higher need that our covariates only partly measure; it is consistent with equitable, need-driven admission rather than evidence of a problem. Supporting this, the gradient is essentially unchanged after birth weight and Apgar are added (see the sensitivity comparison below) — what we would expect if it reflects residual, unmeasured need.
A genuine difference in admission propensity. Alternatively, hospitals serving deprived populations may admit at a lower threshold, or high-risk pregnancies may be concentrated in specialist centres in urban/deprived areas. If any part of the gradient reflects a true difference in access rather than need, that would warrant separate investigation.

These cannot be fully separated with the current model, but there is a direct check available: if morbidity itself rises across IMD quintiles in this cohort — and especially if it rises in ways the model does not adjust for — the unmeasured-need reading is supported.

On this evidence the unmeasured-need reading is well supported: deprivation is acting substantially as a proxy for morbidity our covariates do not fully measure. 4.4.2 Does the deprivation gradient differ by ethnic group?
The models so far constrain the deprivation gradient to be the same in every ethnic group (and equivalently, ethnicity gaps to be the same in every deprivation quintile). A natural follow-up question is whether the two dimensions of inequality compound — for example, whether deprivation carries a steeper penalty for some ethnic groups than others.
To test this, the primary model was refitted with a full ethnicity × deprivation interaction. This is presented as exploratory: the interaction adds 36 parameters, and picking through 36 individual cell contrasts would invite exactly the multiple-comparison problem flagged elsewhere in this report. The primary readout is therefore a single global likelihood-ratio test of whether there is evidence the gradient differs at all, which is one test and carries no multiplicity burden. The within-group estimates below are shown to describe the pattern, not to make claims about any individual group.
The global test does find evidence that the gradient is not uniform: χ²(36) = 65.7, p = 0.0018. But the departure is small. Both information criteria prefer the simpler main-effects model (AIC +6, BIC +405 for the interaction model): with 476,475 births, a likelihood-ratio test is powered to detect departures from uniformity far too small to matter practically. The main-effects model remains the primary specification.








Figure 5: Within-group deprivation gradient: odds of NCC admission for the most vs least deprived quintile, estimated separately for each ethnic group (interaction model, adjusted for gestation, with hospital random effects). Dashed line: no gradient. Dotted line: the pooled gradient from the main-effects model. Intervals are wide for smaller groups — exploratory only.





The pattern behind the global signal (Figure 5) is informative, read descriptively. The only within-group gradient whose interval excludes 1 is White British (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.08–1.18) — slightly steeper than the pooled estimate of 1.1. Several minority groups have point estimates of similar or larger magnitude (Indian, Pakistani, Black), but with intervals spanning 1; others (Bangladeshi, Chinese, Other Asian) point flat or below, with very wide intervals. The imprecision is structural rather than incidental: minority ethnic births are concentrated in the more deprived quintiles, so the least-deprived reference cells are small — 306 Bangladeshi and 376 Chinese births in the least deprived quintile, against tens of thousands of White British.
Two conclusions follow. First, there is no evidence that deprivation carries a steeper penalty for minority ethnic groups — the detectable gradient sits within the White British majority, and the pooled deprivation OR reported by the primary model is dominated by that group. Second, that is a statement about the limits of the data as much as about the world: for the smaller groups the data cannot distinguish a flat gradient from a substantial one in either direction, so absence of evidence here is not evidence of absence. Neither conclusion disturbs the unmeasured-need reading of the main deprivation effect, and the main-effects model remains the primary specification throughout.

text:
4.5 Hospital Variation
Once gestation, ethnicity and deprivation are controlled for, the trust a baby is born in is the largest remaining source of variation in the model: the ICC of 0.317 dwarfs the ethnicity ORs (typically 0.87–1.05) and the deprivation OR (1.08 for most vs least deprived). This should not be read simply as “where a baby is born matters most”: the ICC bundles together at least four things this dataset cannot fully separate:

Genuine practice variation — different clinical thresholds for NCC admission between hospitals.
Reporting variation — MSDS submission completeness varies considerably between providers, and PbR-CC submission is also patchy. The dual-source NCC_Admitted flag mitigates this but does not eliminate it: nationally the CC source captures ~3.8x more NCC admissions than MSDS alone, and that ratio differs by provider.
Case-mix concentration via antenatal referral — high-risk pregnancies are transferred in utero to tertiary centres, so babies born at NICU trusts carry more unmeasured risk than gestation alone records. (Postnatal transfers cannot inflate a delivery trust’s rate in this model: an admission is attributed to the trust where the baby was born, not where the care was given.)
Residual case-mix — gestation alone is a thin proxy for clinical need. The sensitivity model (gestation + birth weight + Apgar) reduces but does not remove this.

The ICC is therefore a useful signal that something at the provider level is driving variation, but it should not be reported as a clean estimate of variation in admission practice. Where it has been possible to decompose it — the funnel-outlier diagnostic — the evidence points to reporting breadth (what gets counted as an NCC day) as the dominant driver at the extremes. Providers in the tails may warrant follow-up, but an extreme estimate could equally reflect submission completeness, referral patterns, local thresholds for late-preterm admission, or case-mix not captured by gestation alone.

3.2 Phase 2: Cox Proportional Hazards with Shared Frailty (on hold)
The planned Phase 2 analysis would fit Cox models with a shared frailty term for delivery trust — the survival analysis analogue of the mixed-effects logistic model — to isolate the timing/delay question from the access question addressed in Phase 1.
This phase is currently paused: the MSDS extract available in this environment does not contain a true day-of-birth field, so hours-from-birth cannot be computed reliably. Once the alternative data environment is in place, the planned specification is:

Primary model: Adjust for gestation, ethnicity, IMD, and delivery unit type (NICU/LNU/SCBU), with hospital frailty
Sensitivity model: Additionally adjust for birth weight and Apgar score
Analysis restricted to births at hospitals with a recognised NNAP neonatal unit

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care
text:
4.1 Key Messages (Phase 1)

Clinical need drives admission. Gestation is by far the strongest predictor — each additional week of gestation roughly 38% lower odds — and ethnicity and deprivation effects are small by comparison. On its central question, the system looks need-led.
No evidence of under-access for Black babies nationally. Admission rates are almost identical to White British (~13.4%), and stay at parity after clinical adjustment — despite Black babies carrying higher average clinical need. This is a reassuring finding in the context of recent maternity reviews (MBRRACE, Ockenden). A per-trust screen found one trust (of 92 testable) with a significantly lower Black admission rate, now flagged for follow-up.
Two groups warrant follow-up. Pakistani babies’ modestly lower odds are largely explained by clinical factors — they move to near-parity once birth weight and Apgar are adjusted for — but the Phase 1 report’s length-of-stay and mortality extensions add convergent Pakistani findings that point to a severity-at-admission follow-up. Chinese babies show around 24% lower odds even after adjustment; this could reflect lower genuine need, upstream maternal-risk differences, statistical fragility in a small group, or under-recording — the data cannot yet separate these, so it is a question rather than a conclusion.
The deprivation gradient looks like need, not inequity. Babies from the most deprived areas have around 9% higher adjusted odds of admission, but a direct check shows morbidity itself rises with deprivation (low birth weight among term babies nearly doubles from least to most deprived). Higher admission is consistent with the system responding to genuinely sicker babies.
Hospital variation is the largest residual signal, but the extremes reflect recording practice. Where a baby is born matters (ICC ~32%); however, diagnostics on the most extreme trusts show they record NCC for 21–40% of term babies (~7% nationally) — a difference in what is counted as critical care in returns, not in admission practice. Standardising what counts as an NCC day in PbR-CC returns is the highest-value quick win; admission-practice comparisons only become reliable after it.
The timing question is still open. Whether some groups wait longer for NCC is a separate question that Phase 1 cannot address; it needs the day-of-birth field unavailable in this environment (Phase 2, on hold).

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
1.1 Key Messages

Clinical need drives admission. Each additional week of gestation reduces the odds of NCC admission by around 38%; ethnicity and deprivation effects are small by comparison. On its central question, the system appears need-led.
There is no evidence of under-admission for Black babies at national level. Odds ratios are approximately 1.04 in both the primary and sensitivity models — essentially parity with White British, despite higher average clinical need. This is a finding about admission rates only, not about the wider quality of care received.
Two groups warrant follow-up. Pakistani babies’ lower odds in the primary model move to near-parity once birth weight and Apgar are added, so are largely explained by case-mix — though the length-of-stay and mortality analyses add further Pakistani findings that together point to a severity-at-admission follow-up. Chinese babies show around 24% lower odds even after adjustment; at least four explanations are consistent with this and the data cannot separate them (see Ethnicity).
The deprivation gradient is consistent with need rather than over-admission. Odds are around 9% higher for the most deprived quintile relative to the least, stable after clinical adjustment, and a direct morbidity check shows clinical need itself rising with deprivation in ways the model does not capture.
Between-trust variation is the largest residual signal (ICC around 32%), but it bundles admission practice with recording practice and cannot be read at face value. The funnel-outlier diagnostic shows the most extreme trusts record NCC for 21–40% of their term babies, against roughly 7% nationally — a recording signature, not an admission-practice one. Standardising what counts as an NCC day in PbR-CC returns is the highest-value data improvement identified by this work.
These results address whether a baby is admitted, not when. The planned Phase 2 analysis of admission timing is on hold pending access to a data environment with a usable date of birth.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.2 Outcome definition (NCC_Admitted)
The outcome flags whether a baby has care recorded as Neonatal Critical Care in either of the two available administrative sources: MSDS MSD402 (provider-submitted neonatal admission records) or PbR-CC (the Payment-by-Results critical-care daily extract, filtered to CC_Type = 'NCC'). A baby is NCC_Admitted = 1 if they appear in either source. The two sources do not agree perfectly: the CC source records roughly 3.8 times more NCC admissions than MSDS alone, and submission completeness for both sources varies between providers. The outcome should therefore be read as “received care recorded as NCC” rather than as a clinically-curated definition of admission to a neonatal critical care cot.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.3 Cohort filter and deprivation vintage
Two further constraints apply to the primary cohort:

Hospital births only. The cohort is restricted to babies whose mother has a recorded MSD301 hospital labour-delivery spell (Mother_Admission_Date IS NOT NULL). This is consistent with the study’s “hospital births in England” frame, but it excludes home births and any births where the labour record did not link in MSDS — the latter is not random across providers.
IMD 2015 vintage. The deprivation field used (IMD_Decile_2015) is derived from the 2015 release of the English Indices of Deprivation. IMD 2019 is now the current vintage, and a 2025 release is anticipated. Some areas have reclassified noticeably since 2015. Findings should be interpreted as applying to the 2015 deprivation classification of the mother’s recorded address.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.6 Birth Weight Data Source
The sensitivity model uses birth weight from MSDS only (Birth_Weight_Grams), not the combined MSDS+CC variable. This avoids differential missingness bias: the CC data has 94% birth weight completeness for NCC babies vs 46% for non-NCC babies, which would artificially inflate NCC rates in complete cases.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.7 Random-effect Grouping
The hierarchical models cluster babies at the level of the submitting NHS trust (3-letter provider code), not the individual delivery site (5-letter code). Two practical considerations drove this:

Coverage. MSDS populates the site-of-delivery field (Org_Site_ID_Actual_Place_Delivery) for ~83% of babies; the remaining ~17% have no site recorded but do have a submitting-trust code (OrgCodeProvider) populated for 100% of records. The no-site cohort is concentrated in 15 large multi-site trusts and is not random with respect to outcome (NCC rate 14.2% vs 11.5% in the with-site cohort), ethnicity (more Pakistani, fewer Indian) or deprivation. Excluding it on a missing-site filter would bias the model.
Hierarchy. Site codes (e.g. RYJ01) sit administratively inside trust codes (e.g. RYJ). Treating “RYJ01” babies and “RYJ-trust-only” babies as independent random-effect groups would double-count trust-level variance and break the exchangeability assumption. Clustering at trust level for everyone keeps a single consistent rung.

The grouping variable is constructed as Delivery_Trust = coalesce(LEFT(Delivery_Site_Code, 3), Submitting_Org_Code), then used as the random-intercept term (1 | Delivery_Trust). For multi-site trusts (Imperial, Leicester, Barts, etc.), within-trust between-site variation is folded into the residual rather than the random effect; the reported ICC is therefore a slightly conservative estimate of between-hospital variation.

2.7.1 Why mixed effects?
A standard regression would treat all 500,000+ babies as independent draws from one giant, uniform hospital. They are not: babies are clustered within trusts, and the baseline likelihood of NCC admission varies widely between trusts — through clinical thresholds, local capacity and reporting practice. Ignoring that clustering has two costs. It understates uncertainty (babies within a hospital partly repeat the same hospital-level information), and it can generate false findings: if an ethnic group happens to be concentrated around hospitals that admit (or report) more, a standard model would attribute the hospital’s behaviour to the group.
The mixed-effects model fixes this by giving each trust its own baseline admission rate (a “random intercept”), with the trust baselines treated as draws from a common distribution. The patient-level effects — ethnicity, deprivation, clinical need — are then estimated with the hospital baseline held constant. So when we report that the most deprived quintile has 9.4% higher odds of admission, it means: for two clinically identical babies born in the same trust, the baby from the most deprived area is 9.4% more likely to be admitted.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
4.4 Implications for Maternity Review

System-level: NCC access for Black babies appears equitable on average nationally. This is a positive finding, though it speaks only to admission — not to the wider quality of maternity or neonatal care.
Hospital-level: Crude Black–White gaps vary between providers, but the formal screen above found only one trust (of 92 testable) with a significantly lower Black admission rate after correction, against three significantly higher. That trust is flagged for a case-mix-standardised follow-up; the rest of the variation is within what chance and case-mix would produce.
Clinical adjustment matters: After adjusting for birth weight and Apgar, Black babies retain slightly higher NCC odds — the pattern expected if the system is responding appropriately to their higher average clinical need.
Contrast with other groups: Pakistani and Chinese babies show lower NCC odds even after clinical adjustment — the groups where follow-up should focus (see Key Message 4 for the candidate explanations).

title: Neonatal Critical Care Access: Preliminary Modelling Results
section: 4.7 Hospital ICC: dominant signal, but mixed sources
text:
4.7 Hospital ICC: dominant signal, but mixed sources
The between-hospital ICC (~32%) is far larger than the ethnicity ORs (typically 0.87–1.05) and the deprivation OR (1.08 for most vs least deprived). It is tempting to read this as “where a baby is born matters most” — but the ICC bundles together at least four things this dataset cannot separate:

Genuine practice variation — different clinical thresholds for NCC admission between hospitals.
Reporting variation — MSDS submission completeness varies considerably between providers, and PbR-CC submission is also patchy. The dual-source NCC_Admitted flag mitigates this but does not eliminate it: nationally the CC source captures ~3.8x more NCC admissions than MSDS alone, and that ratio differs by provider.
Case-mix concentration via antenatal referral — high-risk pregnancies are transferred in utero to tertiary centres, so babies born at NICU trusts carry more unmeasured risk than gestation alone records. (Note that postnatal transfers cannot inflate a delivery trust’s rate in this model: an admission is attributed to the trust where the baby was born, not where the care was given.)
Residual case-mix — gestation alone is a thin proxy for clinical need. The sensitivity model (gestation + birth weight + Apgar) reduces but does not remove this.

The ICC is therefore a useful signal that something at the provider level is driving variation, but it should not be reported as a clean estimate of variation in admission practice.
Hospitals in the tails of the distribution may warrant further investigation, but interpretation should bear in mind that an extreme provider-level estimate could equally reflect a data-completeness issue. Useful follow-up questions include:

Whether the provider’s MSD402 (and CC) submission rate is in line with peers.
Whether the provider receives transfers from a wider network (high “admission” rate as a referral centre).
Whether local clinical thresholds for NCC differ — e.g. routine vs selective admission of late preterm infants.
Whether case-mix not captured by gestation alone (multiplicity, congenital anomaly) drives the apparent effect.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
2.4 Variable selection
This is a causal estimation problem rather than a prediction problem, and that distinction governs the approach to selecting variables. The aim is not to predict NCC admission as accurately as possible; it is to estimate the association of ethnicity and deprivation with admission conditional on clinical need. Each candidate variable is therefore judged first on its causal role, and only then on whether it is usable:

Causal role. A variable is an exposure of interest (ethnicity, IMD — the inequalities being measured), a confounder of need (clinical case-mix that must be adjusted for so that “conditional on need” is meaningful), a mediator (on the causal pathway from exposure to admission, which must not be adjusted for if the total effect is wanted — the “Table 2 fallacy”), or a collider (adjusting for which would introduce bias). Confounders are candidates for adjustment; mediators and colliders are left out, however predictive they are.
Clinical relevance. Among confounders, how strongly the variable drives genuine NCC need.
Completeness. Whether it is recorded for enough of the cohort to use without shrinking or biasing the sample. A near-complete weak confounder can be preferable to a strong but half-missing one — the gestation-versus-birth-weight trade-off below.
Collinearity. Correlation among the adjustment variables inflates the variance of those coefficients, but does not bias the ethnicity/IMD estimates unless a covariate is collinear with ethnicity or IMD. Correlated clinical measures are a reason for parsimony, not a threat to the headline estimates.


2.4.1 Why selection is not data-driven (stepwise / LASSO)
Algorithmic selection — stepwise regression, LASSO, and similar — optimises predictive fit and is blind to causal role. Such a procedure would happily adjust for a mediator (biasing the exposure estimate toward the null), or drop a true confounder because it is collinear with another. For a causal access question this is the wrong tool: it answers “what predicts admission?” when we are asking “is admission equitable conditional on need?”. Selection here is therefore pre-specified on clinical and causal grounds by design. Where robustness to the adjustment set matters, the appropriate check is not a data-driven search but a small set of pre-specified alternative specifications (see Recommendations).

text:
4.6 Hospital Variation: the largest signal, read with care
Once gestation, ethnicity and deprivation are controlled for, the trust a baby is born in is the largest remaining source of variation in the model: the ICC of 0.317 dwarfs the ethnicity ORs (typically 0.87–1.05) and the deprivation OR (1.08 for most vs least deprived). It is tempting to read this as “where a baby is born matters most” — but the ICC bundles together at least four things this dataset cannot fully separate:

Genuine practice variation — different clinical thresholds for NCC admission between hospitals.
Reporting variation — MSDS submission completeness varies considerably between providers, and PbR-CC submission is also patchy. The dual-source NCC_Admitted flag mitigates this but does not eliminate it: nationally the CC source captures ~3.8x more NCC admissions than MSDS alone, and that ratio differs by provider.
Case-mix concentration via antenatal referral — high-risk pregnancies are transferred in utero to tertiary centres, so babies born at NICU trusts carry more unmeasured risk than gestation alone records. (Note that postnatal transfers cannot inflate a delivery trust’s rate in this model: an admission is attributed to the trust where the baby was born, not where the care was given.)
Residual case-mix — gestation alone is a thin proxy for clinical need. The sensitivity model (gestation + birth weight + Apgar) reduces but does not remove this.

The ICC is therefore a useful signal that something at the provider level is driving variation, but it should not be reported as a clean estimate of variation in admission practice. Where we have been able to decompose it — the funnel-outlier diagnostic — the evidence points to reporting breadth (what gets counted as an NCC day) as the dominant driver at the extremes.
Hospitals in the tails of the distribution may warrant further investigation, but interpretation should bear in mind that an extreme provider-level estimate could equally reflect a data-completeness issue. Useful follow-up questions include:

Whether the provider’s MSD402 (and CC) submission rate is in line with peers.
Whether the provider receives transfers from a wider network (high “admission” rate as a referral centre).
Whether local clinical thresholds for NCC differ — e.g. routine vs selective admission of late preterm infants.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
section: 6.1 What adjustment does to the crude picture
text:
6.1 What adjustment does to the crude picture
The Black crude excess is entirely case-mix. After gestation-band adjustment the rate ratio for Black babies is 0.98 (0.95–1.01) — the 25% crude excess in mean stay disappears entirely, because Black babies’ longer average stays reflect their higher preterm rates, not longer stays at a given severity. Combined with the admission model (OR ~1.04) this extends the equitable-access finding: Black babies are admitted at parity and, once admitted, receive the expected quantity of care for their gestation.
Pakistani and Bangladeshi babies stay around 9–10% longer than expected. The two groups with the most interesting admission-model results are also the ones with adjusted stay excesses that survive BH correction: Pakistani 1.09 (1.05–1.12) and Bangladeshi 1.10 (1.04–1.16). For Pakistani babies the direction is notable: this group had ~11% lower adjusted odds of admission, and lower admission propensity combined with longer stays once admitted is the pattern one would expect if the effective admission threshold is higher — the marginal, milder cases don’t get admitted, so those who do are sicker and stay longer. This is a hypothesis, not a demonstration: greater within-gestation-band morbidity (e.g. growth restriction, congenital anomaly rates) would produce the same signature, and this model cannot separate the two. For Bangladeshi babies, whose admission odds were slightly above parity, the threshold reading does not fit, and residual severity is the more natural explanation. Either way, these are again the two groups that a broad “Asian” category would average away.
The deprivation gradient in stay length is almost entirely case-mix. The crude mean gap (10.5 vs 9.0 days, most vs least deprived) shrinks to a residual 3.2% (RR 1.03 (1.01–1.06)) — small, and consistent with the unmeasured-need reading: the model adjusts for gestation band but not for the growth restriction that rises with deprivation within gestation bands.
Trusts vary substantially in recorded stay length. The trust random-intercept SD (0.31 on the log scale) implies a trust one SD above average records ~36% longer stays than expected for its case-mix. This should not be read as pure clinical practice: the funnel diagnostic showed that what gets counted as an NCC day varies markedly between trusts, and that recording breadth flows directly into this outcome. The stay-length measure here is “days carrying an NCC critical-care record”, not independently verified cot-days.






WarningReading length of stay conditional on admission



This analysis conditions on admission, which is itself the outcome of the earlier models. If a group’s admission threshold differs, its admitted babies are a differently-selected slice of the same underlying population — which changes expected stay length without any difference in care received. Rate ratios here should therefore be read jointly with the admission model, never in isolation. The Pakistani finding above is the concrete example: its interpretation depends directly on the admission result.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
7.1 Measuring death in this data
Mirroring the dual-source design of the NCC admission flag, a baby is counted as having died if either source records it: the MSDS death date (deaths known to the maternity service), or — added in a July 2026 extract refresh — a hospital spell in APCS ending with discharge method “died”, which also captures deaths after maternity discharge in any hospital, up to the end of the extract window (30 April 2024). Among 504,392 live births, 1,448 deaths are recorded (2.87 per 1,000): 731 in both sources, 593 in APCS only and 124 in MSDS only. The two sources corroborate each other well — where both record a death, 685 of 731 (94%) agree on the date to within a day — but neither alone is complete: MSDS sees 59% of the combined total and APCS 91%. A further 45 babies recorded as live births in MSDS but coded as stillbirths in APCS were removed as vital-status-uncertain.
Three properties of this flag must be kept in view. First, it means “death recorded in hospital or by the maternity service within the extract window”, not 28-day neonatal mortality. With no day of birth available in this environment, age at death cannot be computed, so no clinically standard mortality window can be constructed. Second, follow-up is uneven: a baby born in March 2024 has around two months of in-window observation against thirteen for an April 2023 birth. In practice this matters little — recorded death rates are flat across birth months (2.6–3.1 per 1,000, with no decline at the end of the year), as expected when most in-hospital infant deaths occur close to birth. Third, deaths outside hospital after discharge are invisible here, and that invisibility need not be evenly distributed across groups.
The flag behaves as clinical reality would predict: rates run from 270 per 1,000 below 28 weeks’ gestation to 0.8 per 1,000 at term — a gradient of roughly 350-fold — and NCC-admitted babies die at 12.3 per 1,000 against 1.6 among the never-admitted.

section: 7.3 What standardisation does to the crude picture
text:
7.3 What standardisation does to the crude picture
The Black crude excess is mostly gestational mix. After standardisation the Black O/E is 1.18 (0.99–1.40) — the crude doubling largely reflects higher preterm rates, the same mechanism as the length-of-stay finding. The residual leans above 1 without reaching significance; MBRRACE, with full death-registration linkage and richer adjustment, does find a genuine residual excess for Black babies, so the near-parity here should be read as limited power and crude adjustment, not as contradicting it.
The Pakistani excess is not gestational mix. Pakistani babies show 80% more recorded deaths than their gestational-age distribution predicts (O/E 1.80 (1.50–2.15), BH-adjusted p < 0.001) — the strongest signal in this section, and consistent with MBRRACE findings of elevated perinatal mortality for babies of Pakistani ethnicity at every gestation, in which congenital anomalies are a documented contributor. Set alongside this report’s other Pakistani findings — around 11% lower adjusted odds of NCC admission, and around 9% longer stays once admitted — a consistent picture emerges of a group with higher within-gestation clinical need whose access does not appear correspondingly higher. All three signals point to the same follow-up: severity at admission (recommendation 6).
The deprivation gradient survives standardisation. The most deprived quintile records 20% more deaths than its gestational mix predicts (O/E 1.20 (1.09–1.32)) and the least deprived 23% fewer (0.77 (0.64–0.92)), a monotone gradient across quintiles. As with the admission-model gradient, this is consistent with deprivation-linked morbidity within gestation bands (growth restriction rises with deprivation even among term babies — see the morbidity check).
One estimate is implausibly low. White Other babies record 37% fewer deaths than expected (O/E 0.63 (0.49–0.80), BH-adjusted p < 0.001). A genuinely lower risk is possible, but this group plausibly includes families with stronger ties abroad, and a death after leaving the country — or after transfer out of NHS hospital care — is invisible to both sources. This is a concrete reminder that ascertainment, as well as risk, can differ by group — which is why this section stays descriptive.






WarningWhat this mortality flag is not



This is not neonatal mortality as nationally defined: no age at death can be computed (no day of birth in this environment), deaths are only visible while in hospital or known to the maternity service, and the observation window is administrative (to 30 April 2024) rather than clinical (28 days). Group comparisons assume ascertainment is equal across groups, which the White Other result suggests may not hold. These figures are an internal consistency check on this dataset’s access findings — for population inequalities in neonatal mortality, MBRRACE-UK perinatal surveillance is the appropriate reference.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
9.1 Key Messages

Clinical need drives admission. Each additional week of gestation reduces the odds of NCC admission by around 38%; ethnicity and deprivation effects are small by comparison. On its central question, the system appears need-led.
There is no evidence of under-admission for Black babies at national level. Odds ratios are approximately 1.04 in both the primary and sensitivity models — essentially parity with White British, despite higher average clinical need. This is a finding about admission rates only, not about the wider quality of care received.
Two groups warrant follow-up. Pakistani babies’ lower odds in the primary model move to near-parity once birth weight and Apgar are added, so are largely explained by case-mix — though the length-of-stay and mortality analyses add further Pakistani findings that together point to a severity-at-admission follow-up. Chinese babies show around 24% lower odds even after adjustment; at least four explanations are consistent with this and the data cannot separate them (see Ethnicity).
The deprivation gradient is consistent with need rather than over-admission. Odds are around 9% higher for the most deprived quintile relative to the least, stable after clinical adjustment, and a direct morbidity check shows clinical need itself rising with deprivation in ways the model does not capture.
Between-trust variation is the largest residual signal (ICC around 32%), but it bundles admission practice with recording practice and cannot be read at face value. The funnel-outlier diagnostic shows the most extreme trusts record NCC for 21–40% of their term babies, against roughly 7% nationally — a recording signature, not an admission-practice one. Standardising what counts as an NCC day in PbR-CC returns is the highest-value data improvement identified by this work.
These results address whether a baby is admitted, not when. The planned Phase 2 analysis of admission timing is on hold pending access to a data environment with a usable date of birth.

text:
10.1 Study Population
{r study_pop, echo=FALSE} n_primary <- nobs(model2) n_sensitivity <- nobs(model3)
Primary analysis: r format(n_primary, big.mark = ",") hospital births in England during financial year 2023/24 with complete data on NCC admission, gestation, ethnicity, IMD quintile, and delivery trust.
Sensitivity analysis: r format(n_sensitivity, big.mark = ",") births (r round(100*n_sensitivity/n_primary, 1)% of primary sample) with additional complete data on birth weight and Apgar 5-minute score.
The cohort is defined by birth in 2023/24, not by NCC activity in 2023/24. Babies enter on the basis of their MSDS birth record (the financial year is derived from year and month of birth); a baby born before April 2023 who continued a neonatal stay into the study year is not included. Critical-care linkage then looks outward from each birth — and is permitted to reach about 30 days into 2024/25 — so that NCC admissions for babies born late in March 2024 are not under-counted; but the linkage never pulls earlier-born babies into the cohort.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.2 Outcome definition (NCC_Admitted)
The outcome flags whether a baby has care recorded as Neonatal Critical Care in either of the two available administrative sources: MSDS MSD402 (provider-submitted neonatal admission records) or PbR-CC (the Payment-by-Results critical-care daily extract, filtered to CC_Type = 'NCC'). A baby is NCC_Admitted = 1 if they appear in either source. The two sources do not agree perfectly: the CC source records roughly 3.8 times more NCC admissions than MSDS alone, and submission completeness for both sources varies between providers. The outcome should therefore be read as “received care recorded as NCC” rather than as a clinically-curated definition of admission to a neonatal critical care cot.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.3 Cohort filter and deprivation vintage
Two further constraints apply to the primary cohort:

Hospital births only. The cohort is restricted to babies whose mother has a recorded MSD301 hospital labour-delivery spell (Mother_Admission_Date IS NOT NULL). This is consistent with the study’s “hospital births in England” frame, but it excludes home births and any births where the labour record did not link in MSDS — the latter is not random across providers.
IMD 2015 vintage. The deprivation field used (IMD_Decile_2015) is derived from the 2015 release of the English Indices of Deprivation. IMD 2019 is now the current vintage, and a 2025 release is anticipated. Some areas have reclassified noticeably since 2015. Findings should be interpreted as applying to the 2015 deprivation classification of the mother’s recorded address.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.4 Variable selection
This is a causal estimation problem rather than a prediction problem, and that distinction governs the approach to selecting variables. The aim is not to predict NCC admission as accurately as possible; it is to estimate the association of ethnicity and deprivation with admission conditional on clinical need. Each candidate variable is therefore judged first on its causal role, and only then on whether it is usable:

Causal role. A variable is an exposure of interest (ethnicity, IMD — the inequalities being measured), a confounder of need (clinical case-mix that must be adjusted for so that “conditional on need” is meaningful), a mediator (on the causal pathway from exposure to admission, which must not be adjusted for if the total effect is wanted — the “Table 2 fallacy”), or a collider (adjusting for which would introduce bias). Confounders are candidates for adjustment; mediators and colliders are left out, however predictive they are.
Clinical relevance. Among confounders, how strongly the variable drives genuine NCC need.
Completeness. Whether it is recorded for enough of the cohort to use without shrinking or biasing the sample. A near-complete weak confounder can be preferable to a strong but half-missing one — the gestation-versus-birth-weight trade-off below.
Collinearity. Correlation among the adjustment variables inflates the variance of those coefficients, but does not bias the ethnicity/IMD estimates unless a covariate is collinear with ethnicity or IMD. Correlated clinical measures are a reason for parsimony, not a threat to the headline estimates.


10.4.1 Why selection is not data-driven (stepwise / LASSO)
Algorithmic selection — stepwise regression, LASSO, and similar — optimises predictive fit and is blind to causal role. Such a procedure would happily adjust for a mediator (biasing the exposure estimate toward the null), or drop a true confounder because it is collinear with another. For a causal access question this is the wrong tool: it answers “what predicts admission?” when we are asking “is admission equitable conditional on need?”. Selection here is therefore pre-specified on clinical and causal grounds by design. Where robustness to the adjustment set matters, the appropriate check is not a data-driven search but a small set of pre-specified alternative specifications (see Recommendations).

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.5 Statistical Approach
We fitted three models:

Model 1 (Fixed effects only): Standard logistic regression adjusting for gestation, ethnicity, and deprivation. Retained as a reference point; estimates are in the technical appendix.
Model 2 (Mixed effects, gestation only): Hierarchical logistic regression with random intercepts for delivery trust, adjusting only for gestation among clinical covariates \[\text{logit}(P[\text{NCC}]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_3 \text{IMD} + u_j\] where \(u_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\) represents the random effect for delivery trust \(j\). Reported because it uses the maximum sample size (gestation is near-completely observed).
Model 3 (Mixed effects, full clinical adjustment): Adds birth weight and Apgar 5-minute score to Model 2’s specification \[\text{logit}(P[\text{NCC}]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Gestation} + \beta_2 \text{BirthWeight} + \beta_3 \text{Apgar} + \beta_4 \text{Ethnicity} + \beta_5 \text{IMD} + u_j\]

Conceptually Model 3 is the preferred specification — it adjusts for the clinical case-mix that drives NCC need rather than relying on gestation alone — and we lead the interpretation with its results. Model 2 is reported in parallel because of its larger sample (gestation is observed for nearly all births, whereas birth weight and Apgar are observed for r round(100*n_sensitivity/n_primary, 1)% of the primary sample). Where the two models disagree (notably for Pakistani and Indian ethnic groups), the disagreement itself is informative and is discussed below.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.6 Birth Weight Data Source
The sensitivity model uses birth weight from MSDS only (Birth_Weight_Grams), not the combined MSDS+CC variable. This avoids differential missingness bias: the CC data has 94% birth weight completeness for NCC babies vs 46% for non-NCC babies, which would artificially inflate NCC rates in complete cases.

title: Inequalities in Access to Neonatal Critical Care: Phase 1 Modelling Results
text:
10.7 Random-effect Grouping
The hierarchical models cluster babies at the level of the submitting NHS trust (3-letter provider code), not the individual delivery site (5-letter code). Two practical considerations drove this:

Coverage. MSDS populates the site-of-delivery field (Org_Site_ID_Actual_Place_Delivery) for ~83% of babies; the remaining ~17% have no site recorded but do have a submitting-trust code (OrgCodeProvider) populated for 100% of records. The no-site cohort is concentrated in 15 large multi-site trusts and is not random with respect to outcome (NCC rate 14.2% vs 11.5% in the with-site cohort), ethnicity (more Pakistani, fewer Indian) or deprivation. Excluding it on a missing-site filter would bias the model.
Hierarchy. Site codes (e.g. RYJ01) sit administratively inside trust codes (e.g. RYJ). Treating “RYJ01” babies and “RYJ-trust-only” babies as independent random-effect groups would double-count trust-level variance and break the exchangeability assumption. Clustering at trust level for everyone keeps a single consistent rung.

The grouping variable is constructed as Delivery_Trust = coalesce(LEFT(Delivery_Site_Code, 3), Submitting_Org_Code), then used as the random-intercept term (1 | Delivery_Trust). For multi-site trusts (Imperial, Leicester, Barts, etc.), within-trust between-site variation is folded into the residual rather than the random effect; the reported ICC is therefore a slightly conservative estimate of between-hospital variation.

10.7.1 Why mixed effects?
A standard regression would treat all 500,000+ babies as independent draws from one giant, uniform hospital. They are not: babies are clustered within trusts, and the baseline likelihood of NCC admission varies widely between trusts — through clinical thresholds, local capacity and reporting practice. Ignoring that clustering has two costs. It understates uncertainty (babies within a hospital partly repeat the same hospital-level information), and it can generate false findings: if an ethnic group happens to be concentrated around hospitals that admit (or report) more, a standard model would attribute the hospital’s behaviour to the group.
The mixed-effects model fixes this by giving each trust its own baseline admission rate (a “random intercept”), with the trust baselines treated as draws from a common distribution. The patient-level effects — ethnicity, deprivation, clinical need — are then estimated with the hospital baseline held constant. So when we report that the most deprived quintile has 9.4% higher odds of admission, it means: for two clinically identical babies born in the same trust, the baby from the most deprived area is 9.4% more likely to be admitted.

text:
27.1 Measuring death in this data
Mirroring the dual-source design of the NCC admission flag, a baby is counted as having died if either source records it: the MSDS death date (deaths known to the maternity service), or — added in a July 2026 extract refresh — a hospital spell in APCS ending with discharge method “died”, which also captures deaths after maternity discharge in any hospital, up to the end of the extract window (30 April 2024). Among r format(a5b$n_cohort, big.mark = ",") live births, r format(n_deaths, big.mark = ",") deaths are recorded (r sprintf("%.2f", a5b$crude_overall$rate) per 1,000): r format(n_both, big.mark = ",") in both sources, r format(n_apcs_only, big.mark = ",") in APCS only and r n_msds_only in MSDS only. The two sources corroborate each other well — where both record a death, r a5b$concordance$within_1_day of r a5b$concordance$n_both_dates (r percent(a5b$concordance$within_1_day / a5b$concordance$n_both_dates, accuracy = 1)) agree on the date to within a day — but neither alone is complete: MSDS sees r pct_msds of the combined total and APCS r pct_apcs. A further r a5b$n_sb_discordant babies recorded as live births in MSDS but coded as stillbirths in APCS were removed as vital-status-uncertain.
Three properties of this flag must be kept in view. First, it means “death recorded in hospital or by the maternity service within the extract window”, not 28-day neonatal mortality. With no day of birth available in this environment, age at death cannot be computed, so no clinically standard mortality window can be constructed. Second, follow-up is uneven: a baby born in March 2024 has around two months of in-window observation against thirteen for an April 2023 birth. In practice this matters little — recorded death rates are flat across birth months (2.6–3.1 per 1,000, with no decline at the end of the year), as expected when most in-hospital infant deaths occur close to birth. Third, deaths outside hospital after discharge are invisible here, and that invisibility need not be evenly distributed across groups.
The flag behaves as clinical reality would predict: rates run from r sprintf("%.0f", a5b$crude_gest$rate[1]) per 1,000 below 28 weeks’ gestation to r sprintf("%.1f", a5b$crude_gest$rate[5]) per 1,000 at term — a gradient of roughly 350-fold — and NCC-admitted babies die at r sprintf("%.1f", a5b$crude_ncc$rate[a5b$crude_ncc$NCC_Admitted == 1]) per 1,000 against r sprintf("%.1f", a5b$crude_ncc$rate[a5b$crude_ncc$NCC_Admitted == 0]) among the never-admitted.

## What standardisation does to the crude picture

The Black crude excess is mostly gestational mix. After standardisation the Black O/E is `r fmt_oe(oe_black)` — the crude doubling largely reflects higher preterm rates, the same mechanism as the length-of-stay finding. The residual leans above 1 without reaching significance; MBRRACE, with full death-registration linkage and richer adjustment, does find a genuine residual excess for Black babies, so the near-parity here should be read as limited power and crude adjustment, not as contradicting it.

The Pakistani excess is not gestational mix. Pakistani babies show `r round(oe_pak$OE * 100 - 100)`% more recorded deaths than their gestational-age distribution predicts (O/E `r fmt_oe(oe_pak)`, BH-adjusted p < 0.001) — the strongest signal in this section, and consistent with MBRRACE findings of elevated perinatal mortality for babies of Pakistani ethnicity at every gestation, in which congenital anomalies are a documented contributor. Set alongside this report's other Pakistani findings — around 11% lower adjusted odds of NCC admission, and around 9% longer stays once admitted — a consistent picture emerges of a group with higher within-gestation clinical need whose access does not appear correspondingly higher. All three signals point to the same follow-up: severity at admission (recommendation 6).

The deprivation gradient survives standardisation. The most deprived quintile records `r round(oe_imd1$OE * 100 - 100)`% more deaths than its gestational mix predicts (O/E `r fmt_oe(oe_imd1)`) and the least deprived `r abs(round(oe_imd5$OE * 100 - 100))`% fewer (`r fmt_oe(oe_imd5)`), a monotone gradient across quintiles. As with the [admission-model gradient](#deprivation), this is consistent with deprivation-linked morbidity *within* gestation bands (growth restriction rises with deprivation even among term babies — see the [morbidity check](#imd-morbidity)).

One estimate is implausibly low. White Other babies record `r abs(round(oe_wo$OE * 100 - 100))`% *fewer* deaths than expected (O/E `r fmt_oe(oe_wo)`, BH-adjusted p < 0.001). A genuinely lower risk is possible, but this group plausibly includes families with stronger ties abroad, and a death after leaving the country — or after transfer out of NHS hospital care — is invisible to both sources. This is a concrete reminder that ascertainment, as well as risk, can differ by group — which is why this section stays descriptive.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What this mortality flag is not
This is not neonatal mortality as nationally defined: no age at death can be computed (no day of birth in this environment), deaths are only visible while in hospital or known to the maternity service, and the observation window is administrative (to 30 April 2024) rather than clinical (28 days). Group comparisons assume ascertainment is equal across groups, which the White Other result suggests may not hold. These figures are an internal consistency check on this dataset's access findings — for population inequalities in neonatal mortality, MBRRACE-UK perinatal surveillance is the appropriate reference.
:::

# Recommendations

The analysis is reassuring on its headline question — no signal of national under-access for Black babies — but it surfaces concrete follow-ups. In rough priority order:

1. Standardise what counts as an "NCC day" in PbR-CC returns. The funnel diagnostic shows the most extreme provider variation is recording breadth, not admission practice: outlier trusts record NCC for 21–40% of their term babies against ~7% nationally. A tighter definition — or an audit of the outlier trusts' returns — would sharpen every downstream use of this data, including the ICC and any future benchmarking.

2. Improve completeness of birth weight and Apgar in MSDS. Jointly complete for under half the cohort, this is the single biggest constraint on case-mix adjustment — it is why the primary model must lean on gestation alone.

3. Follow up the one trust flagged for lower Black admission (identity held internally) with a case-mix-standardised check — a per-trust Black observed/expected ratio — before drawing any conclusion about access.

4. Investigate the Chinese-group gap. Around 24% lower adjusted odds with four candidate explanations this data cannot separate; richer clinical covariates or direct provider engagement would be needed to distinguish need from access or recording.

5. Extend to outcomes and timing. Length of stay and a descriptive mortality look are now analysed above ([stay length](#length-of-stay), [mortality](#mortality)) — both add Pakistani findings that sharpen the case for the Phase 2 timing analysis once the day-of-birth data environment is available. A definitive mortality analysis needs linked death registrations (MBRRACE territory), not this extract.

6. Follow up the Pakistani stay-length excess. Fewer admissions plus longer stays once admitted is consistent with a higher effective admission threshold, but equally with greater within-gestation morbidity; distinguishing them needs severity-at-admission data (care level at day 1, organ support) — a planned extension.

# Limitations

1. Clinical covariate completeness: Birth weight is recorded for ~46% of births and Apgar for ~79%; jointly they limit the sensitivity model to under half the cohort. The primary model uses gestation alone to preserve sample size.

2. Single year of data: Results may not generalise to other time periods.

3. Residual confounding: While ethnicity is now disaggregated (e.g., Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi separately), within-group heterogeneity remains. Black ethnicities are still grouped together in the model.

4. Selection bias: Analysis restricted to births with complete data (`r round(100 * nobs(model2) / nrow(ncc_data), 1)`% of all births) — though the retained share is high and similar across providers (see the funnel diagnostic).

5. Outcome definition: "NCC admission" is whatever providers record as NCC in two administrative sources, and the funnel diagnostic shows the breadth of that recording varies materially between providers. The outcome is best read as "received care recorded as NCC", not "occupied a critical care cot".
